title: 25 Things to Do to Move On From a Breakup
h1: 25 Things to Do to Move On From a Breakup (Starting Today)
description: Need things to do to move on from a breakup? Try these 25 practical ideas for the first days, the weeks after and the months ahead as you rebuild your life.
keyword: things to do to move on from a breakup
excerpt: A practical list of 25 things you can actually do, from the first rough days to rebuilding your routine and rediscovering who you are on your own.
intro:
After a breakup, advice like "just give it time" can feel frustrating. Time does help, but you also want something to do with all that restless energy, sadness and empty space. That's what this list is for. These are concrete things to do to move on from a breakup, organized by stage, so you can pick whatever fits where you are right now.

Some ideas are about getting through the toughest first days. Others help you rebuild routines, reconnect with friends and rediscover what makes you, you. You don't need to do all 25. Choose a handful, start small and come back to the list whenever you need a next step.
body:
How to use this list

Healing after a breakup isn't linear. You might feel ready for a new hobby one week and want to stay under a blanket the next. Both are okay. Think of this list as a menu rather than a checklist. If a suggestion feels impossible today, skip it and pick something smaller. Progress is progress, even when it looks like eating a proper meal and going to bed on time.

In the first few days: get through it gently

1. Let yourself feel it

Cry, journal, vent to a friend or sit with the sadness for a while. Pushing feelings down usually makes them come back stronger later. Give yourself permission to be upset.

2. Cover the basics

Eat something nourishing, drink water, shower and try to sleep. These sound small, but heartbreak can make them feel huge. Taking care of your body gives you a little more emotional strength.

3. Tell a few trusted people

Let close friends or family know what happened so they can check in on you. You don't have to explain every detail. A simple "We broke up and I'm having a hard time" is enough.

4. Pause contact with your ex

Constant texting keeps the wound open. If you can, take a break from contact for a while. If you share kids, a home or a workplace, keep communication short and practical.

5. Mute their social media

Checking their profile will almost always make you feel worse. Mute, unfollow or archive, whatever helps you resist the urge to scroll.

In the first few weeks: create space and structure

6. Box up reminders

Gather photos, gifts and their belongings and put them somewhere out of sight. Return anything that's theirs with a quick, polite drop-off or by asking a friend to help.

7. Build a simple daily routine

Breakups disrupt your rhythm. A basic routine, such as waking at the same time, having a morning walk, working, cooking dinner and winding down, gives your days a stable shape.

8. Spend more time with friends

Say yes to invitations, even short ones. Plan movie nights, walks and dinners. Friends remind you that you're loved and give you a break from replaying the breakup.

9. Write it out

Journaling helps you untangle your thoughts. Try prompts like "What I miss," "What I don't miss" and "What I want next time." Seeing your thoughts on paper often makes them feel more manageable.

10. Write the letter you'll never send

Pour everything you wish you could say into a letter to your ex, then keep it, delete it or tear it up. It's a release valve, not a message.

11. Move your body

A walk, a run, a dance class, yoga, lifting weights: any movement you enjoy can lift your mood and burn off restless energy. Exercise also gives you something to be proud of each day.

Tip: Have a plan for the hardest times of day. For many people that's late at night or weekend mornings. Line up a podcast, a friend to call or an activity so you're not left alone with your thoughts at your lowest moments.

12. Limit alcohol and late-night decisions

A drink or two might feel comforting, but alcohol tends to amplify sadness and makes late-night texts to your ex much more likely. Protect your future self.

Over the next month or two: rediscover yourself

13. Spend intentional time alone

"Me time" is different from isolating. Take yourself to a café, a museum or a movie. Learn to enjoy your own company again. It builds confidence and reminds you that you're complete on your own.

14. Pick up an old hobby

Is there something you loved before the relationship but let slide? Painting, gaming, playing an instrument, hiking, reading: return to it. It reconnects you with who you were before.

15. Try something completely new

Sign up for a class you've always been curious about, like pottery, climbing, a language or improv. New activities create new memories that have nothing to do with your ex.

16. Refresh your space

Rearrange furniture, buy new bedding, add plants or repaint a wall. Changing your environment signals a fresh start, especially if you shared the space.

17. Reconnect with people you drifted from

Relationships can take up a lot of time. Reach out to friends you haven't seen in a while. Many will be happy to hear from you.

18. Plan something to look forward to

A weekend trip, a concert, a day out with friends: having something on the calendar gives you a little spark of anticipation during hard weeks.

19. Volunteer or help someone

Helping others shifts your focus outward and reminds you of your value. Animal shelters, food banks and community events are often looking for volunteers.

Over the longer term: reflect and grow

20. Identify what you actually miss

Is it them, or the companionship, the routine, the feeling of being chosen? Naming what you miss helps you meet those needs in healthy ways and clarifies what you want in a future partner.

21. Reflect on lessons, kindly

What did this relationship teach you about what you need, what you offer and what you won't accept again? Focus on growth, not blame, toward them or yourself.

22. Set a personal goal

Train for a 5K, save for a trip, finish a project, learn a skill. Working toward something meaningful builds confidence and gives your energy a direction.

23. Practice gratitude

Each night, write down three things that went okay that day. It trains your attention toward the good parts of your life, which are still there even when you're hurting.

24. Talk to a professional if you're stuck

If sadness lasts for many weeks, affects your sleep or work, or you feel hopeless, a licensed therapist can help. There's no breakup too "small" to deserve support.

25. Wait for the right time to date again

Dating to fill a gap or make your ex jealous usually backfires. You'll know you're closer to ready when you can think about your ex without a wave of pain and you're genuinely curious about meeting new people.

Tip: Keep a "progress note" on your phone. Every time you notice a small win, like not checking their profile or laughing all evening, write it down. On hard days, reread it to remember how far you've come.

Things to avoid while you heal

  • Constant checking: Their social media, their friends' posts, their online status.
  • Asking mutual friends for updates: It keeps you tied to their life instead of yours.
  • Rebound decisions: Big moves or new relationships made mainly to avoid feeling sad.
  • Isolating for long stretches: Some alone time is healthy; weeks of hiding is not.
  • Harsh self-talk: Breakups don't mean you're unlovable. Talk to yourself like you'd talk to a friend.

When you'll know you're moving on

You'll probably notice it gradually. You'll realize you haven't thought about them all morning. A song that used to wreck you will just be a song. You'll get excited about your own plans again. That's what moving on looks like: not forgetting, but no longer being held back.

For a deeper, step-by-step approach, read our guide on how to move on after a breakup. You might also find help in how to get over a broken heart, how to forget someone and how to deal with loneliness. Explore more in our breakups section.

The bottom line

Moving on from a breakup is built from small actions: a meal, a phone call, a walk, a new class, an honest journal entry. Choose a few ideas from this list, be patient with the hard days and celebrate the good ones. Bit by bit, you'll build a life that feels like yours again.
takeaways: Treat this list as a menu; choose a few ideas that fit where you are right now.
In the first days, focus on feeling your feelings, covering the basics and pausing contact.
Routines, friends, movement and journaling help you through the first weeks.
Rediscover yourself with old hobbies, new classes and intentional time alone.
If sadness lasts many weeks or affects daily life, a licensed therapist can help.

faq.q: What is the fastest way to move on from a breakup?
faq.a: There is no true shortcut, but some steps help a lot: pausing contact with your ex, muting their social media, leaning on friends, keeping a routine and filling your time with activities you enjoy. Letting yourself feel the sadness instead of suppressing it also tends to help you heal more completely.

faq.q: What should you not do after a breakup?
faq.a: Avoid constantly checking your ex's social media, asking mutual friends for updates, sending late-night messages, isolating for long stretches and making big decisions just to avoid sadness. Also be careful with alcohol, which often intensifies low moods and leads to choices you regret.

faq.q: How do I keep myself busy after a breakup?
faq.a: Build a simple routine, schedule time with friends, exercise, return to old hobbies, try a new class, volunteer, refresh your living space and plan something to look forward to. Mixing social activities with some intentional alone time keeps your days full without avoiding your feelings entirely.

faq.q: Is it normal to still be sad months after a breakup?
faq.a: Yes, especially after a long or meaningful relationship. Healing often comes in waves, and anniversaries or reminders can bring feelings back. If sadness is constant, affects your sleep or work, or you feel hopeless, consider talking with a licensed therapist for extra support.
